The question is whether this is the direction we want. Anyway, the techniques: 1, eliminate store-and-forward delay. Store and forward delay means first you have to receive the whole message before you can forward it. Techniques to reduce it: - a, segment, the message, forward per segment. Here you also need to commit to the segments somehow, e.g. sign them - b, cut-through forwarding, which means preprocessing the header and starting forwarding based on that 2, Reduce duplicates when bandwidth constrained. E.g. see my writup on push-pull phase transition. 3, Segment, and erasure code, diffusing ECd segments on multiple path. Here you can use 1D RS, 2D RS as I did in my simuations, or RLC. excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<cskiraly> re: **@justindrake**
> What's the plan for >10 MiB blocks? Should the max message size be a function of gas limit (as opposed to being hardcoded)?
The p2p techniques to diffuse large messages are quite well known. The question is whether this is the direction we want. Anyway, the techniques:

1, eliminate store-and-forward delay. Store and forward delay means first you have to receive the whole message before you can forward it. Techniques to reduce it:
 - a, segment, the message, forward per segment. Here you also need to commit to the segments somehow, e.g. sign them
 - b, cut-through forwarding, which means preprocessing the header and starting forwarding based on that

2, Reduce duplicates when bandwidth constrained. E.g. see my writup on push-pull phase transition.

3, Segment, and erasure code, diffusing ECd segments on multiple path. Here you can use 1D RS, 2D RS as I did in my simuations, or RLC. There are slight differences, but the essence is that you cut the tail of the delay distribution, leading to stricter timings overall.

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<ben_a_adams> re: **@cskiraly**
> The p2p techniques to diffuse large messages are quite well known. The question is whether this is the direction we want. Anyway, the techniques:

1, eliminate store-and-forward delay. Store and forward delay means first you have to receive the whole message before you can forward it. Techniques to reduce it:
 - a, segment, the message, forward per segment. Here you also need to commit to the segments somehow, e.g. sign them
 - b, cut-through forwarding, which means preprocessing the header and starting forwarding based on that

2, Reduce duplicates when bandwidth constrained. E.g. see my writup on push-pull phase transition.

3, Segment, and erasure code, diffusing ECd segments on multiple path. Here you can use 1D RS, 2D RS as I did in my simuations, or RLC. There are slight differences, but the essence is that you cut the tail of the delay distribution, leading to stricter timings overall.
Segmenting also smells a little like smaller faster blocks 😉

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<cskiraly> re: **@ben_a_adams**
> Segmenting also smells a little like smaller faster blocks 😉
Indeed, I'm not saying solve this at the networking layer is the ideal solution. The networking layer has no idea of what's in the message, which leads to inefficiencies. Smaller blocks however means more overhead in other parts of the system, such as attestation traffic, attestation processing, fork choice, etc.

If you want to speed timeframes up for attestations as well, you might have to start pipelining, which interacts with fork choice logic. IMHO long term it's better to have a finer granularity (i.e. smaller blocks and better pipelining). But short term, supporting larger message sizes is easier, and beneficial even well below 10MB. IMHO benefits would start to show on the mainnet well below 1MB.

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: There are some cases where very large preimages need to be posted in OP Stack fault proofs (for data which isn't from blobs like L1 receipts). It's a corner case that would only be hit by someone being malicious and we have a system which allows that data to be posted across multiple transactions (albeit it's very expensive).

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: And actually for posting data, the maximum transaction rlp size is the main limiting factor. It's enforced out of protocol but it's a very effective cap since nearly every node refusing to gossip tx above that size.

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: The biggest transactions we send are L1 contract upgrades because we can bundle a bunch of chain upgrades into a single tx which simplifies the signing process. And because of the way OP Stack upgrades work that requires very little call data but burns quite a lot of gas.

excerpts.author: ben_a_adams
excerpts.content: Is about 128kB max tx size by default? though locally configured on node (Mempool accept size)

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: Yeah something like that. I'm always surprised at how small it is when I bump into it (but makes sense given the impact on gossip).

excerpts.author: ben_a_adams
excerpts.content: How much gas would need to be spent in tx to use this data? (Not post it)

excerpts.author: ben_a_adams
excerpts.content: Would it be > 5MGas?

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: For posting large preimges, I'm not sure of exact numbers but it's explicitly designed to be able to post in small increments. So it wouldn't break if you limited the tx to 5MGas - we'd just have to split it across more transactions.  And my memory is that it hits the tx size limit before gas usage becomes a consideration so it may not make any difference at all.

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: Contract upgrade tx for large systems (like L2s but potentially big apps as well) would be the case I'd be most worried about. They are very rare so wouldn't show up as people regularly using large tx but life becomes *way* more complex if you can't upgrade the system atomically. I would expect a 5Mgas tx limit to cause problems for upgrading OP Stack chains - even if we only upgraded one chain per tx.
